symptoms: Global-route overflow > 0 in specific GCells; congestion map shows red hotspots, often at macro edges or between macro channels
Track utilization 80-95%+ in localized regions while global utilization is moderate; detail router produces detours and spacing DRCs
After routing, timing degrades specifically on nets that traverse congested regions (long detour wirelength), distinguishing congestion-induced timing failure from logic-depth-induced timing failure

candidate_causes.cause: Macro placement creates narrow routing channels (macros too close, or pins oriented away from core)
candidate_causes.distinguishing_check: Overlay congestion map on floorplan: if hotspots align with macro edges AND halos are < 3-5um, it is macro-channel congestion. Rotate/re-position macro and re-run global route; if overflow drops >50%, confirmed.
candidate_causes.typical_fix: Increase macro halo/channel width, rotate macro to face core, move macro toward die edge

candidate_causes.cause: Standard-cell density too high locally (utilization > 80% in hotspot)
candidate_causes.distinguishing_check: Cell density map colocated with congestion hotpot: if density >80% in a red region, it is cell-density congestion. Apply placement blockage or density screen; if overflow reduces, confirmed.
candidate_causes.typical_fix: Add partial placement blockage, reduce utilization target, cell spreading

candidate_causes.cause: Pin-access congestion at advanced nodes (≤7nm, 6-track/5-track cells)
candidate_causes.distinguishing_check: At 7nm/5nm, if M1 pin access legal vias are scarce and congestion concentrates exactly at cell boundaries rather than macro edges, it is pin-access congestion — unique to ≤7nm. 28nm rarely sees this. Confirm with pin-access report.
candidate_causes.typical_fix: Use cell library with better pin access, legalizer-friendly cell variants, MOL routing

candidate_causes.cause: High-fanout nets (clock, reset, scan-enable) consuming a disproportionate share of tracks
candidate_causes.distinguishing_check: If overflow is not co-located with high cell density but rather radiates from a high-fanout source, check clock/reset buffer tree. At ≤7nm, clock tree can consume 5-15% of routing capacity. Clone driver or insert buffers.
candidate_causes.typical_fix: Buffer-tree re-balancing, fanout cloning, route clock on upper layers with NDR

candidate_causes.cause: Power grid over-dense, consuming routing tracks in a layer band
candidate_causes.distinguishing_check: If overflow is uniform across a horizontal or vertical band matching power strap pitch, it is PG-grid congestion. Check strap pitch vs. track availability; if reducing strap density (with IR-drop signoff) relieves congestion, confirmed.
candidate_causes.typical_fix: Stagger power stripes, reduce stripe density, widen upper-layer straps to compensate

candidate_causes.cause: Over-the-block routing demanded but block is a hard macro with no feedthrough
candidate_causes.distinguishing_check: Nets routed over hard macros in hotspot regions with no pre-placed jumper cells; overflow concentrated directly over macro footprint. Fix requires macro re-floorplan or block-level redesign.
candidate_causes.typical_fix: Move macro, or accept routing over macro if metal stack allows

ordering_rationale: Veterans check cheapest-first: density map (minutes) → macro halo inspection (minutes) → fanout/pin-access check (minutes) → power-grid band analysis (hours) → full floorplan revision (days), because 90% of congestion is resolved by the first three checks.
classic_trap: Engineers re-run detailed routing with higher effort hoping the router 'finds a way', when the root cause is floorplan/macro placement. Routing tweaks never fix a structurally unroutable region — you burn hours/days on iterations that cannot succeed.

symptoms: Negative slack on reg-to-reg paths; WNS/LWS reported in STA summary
Slack concentrated in a few paths (few worst offenders) OR spread across thousands of paths (systemic)
After CTS, setup violations appear correlated with specific clock domains or skew groups

candidate_causes.cause: Long combinational logic depth (excessive cell delay, many logic levels)
candidate_causes.distinguishing_check: report_timing -path_type full_clock: if Logic Delay % > 70% of path delay and Logic Levels is high, it is logic-bound. If Net Delay % > 50%, it is not this cause.
candidate_causes.typical_fix: Logic restructuring, cell upsizing (X1->X4), Vt swap to low-Vt, pipeline insertion

candidate_causes.cause: Poor placement: cells physically far apart, large bounding box
candidate_causes.distinguishing_check: In setup path characteristics table: if Net Delay % > 50% and Bounding Box Size is large, or cells span multiple PBlocks/clock regions, it is placement-bound. Check physical location cross-probe.
candidate_causes.typical_fix: Placement optimization, move critical cells closer, add placement guide/region constraint

candidate_causes.cause: High-fanout net with weak driver (slew degradation)
candidate_causes.distinguishing_check: Cumulative Fanout > 50 on a net in the failing path, and transition time violates slew limit. Driver cell cannot charge net fast enough.
candidate_causes.typical_fix: Insert bufffer/inverter tree, clone driver, split fanout

candidate_causes.cause: Clock skew working against the path (launch early, capture late)
candidate_causes.distinguishing_check: In path report, if Clock Skew component is positive (capture later than launch) AND it accounts for a significant fraction of slack, useful skew can help. For hold-sensitive designs, check if useful skew was already pushed to the limit.
candidate_causes.typical_fix: Useful skew (delay capture clock), CTS re-balance, adjust skew groups

candidate_causes.cause: SLR crossing in multi-die (SSI) devices
candidate_causes.distinguishing_check: On SSI devices, if failing paths cross SLR boundaries (SLR Crossings column in report_design_analysis), net delay penalty is structural. Unique to SSI/stacked-die.
candidate_causes.typical_fix: Floorplan to keep timing-critical paths within one SLR, use SLR-aware placement constraints

candidate_causes.cause: Aggressive clock uncertainty / overly tight constraint
candidate_causes.distinguishing_check: If slack violation magnitude equals approximately the clock uncertainty value, and the path itself has comfortable cell+net delay, the constraint is too tight. Compare against design intent.
candidate_causes.typical_fix: Relax clock uncertainty (with justification), correct SDC, remove erroneous exceptions

ordering_rationale: Veteran first runs report_design_analysis to split logic-bound vs net-bound (minutes) — this single check determines whether the fix is synthesis/upsize (cheap) or floorplan/placement (expensive). Then check fanout, then skew, then constraints.
classic_trap: Blindly upsizing cells on a net-delay-dominated path — adds area and power but does not fix wirelength. Conversely, spreading cells to fix congestion can worsen setup by lengthening wires. The classic error is treating all setup violations identically.

symptoms: Negative hold slack, often appearing AFTER CTS (clock skews exposed)
Hold violations clustered on short, fast paths (zero-cycle, back-to-back flip-flops)
Hold violations correlated with useful-skew setup fixes (every ps of setup help costs hold)

candidate_causes.cause: Data path too fast relative to clock (very short combinational path, strong cells)
candidate_causes.distinguishing_check: report_timing -hold: if cell delay components are tiny (ps range) and net delay is minimal, it is a fast-data-path hold violation. Zero-delay paths (direct FF-to-FF) are the canonical case.
candidate_causes.typical_fix: Insert delay buffers on data path ONLY (~50-100ps per buffer), downsize cells, use high-Vt cells

candidate_causes.cause: Positive clock skew introduced by CTS or useful-skew setup fix
candidate_causes.distinguishing_check: Path report shows positive skew (capture arrives earlier than launch) contributing to hold violation. If you recently applied useful skew for setup, hold degradation is expected and symmetric.
candidate_causes.typical_fix: Reduce positive skew on that path, add delay on data path to compensate, adjust skew groups

candidate_causes.cause: Multicycle path incorrectly constrained (effectively a hold issue on a path intended as MC)
candidate_causes.distinguishing_check: If the violating path is logically a multicycle path but SDC lacks set_multicycle_path, hold checker treats it as single-cycle. Review SDC against RTL intent.
candidate_causes.typical_fix: Correct SDC with set_multicycle_path, add -hold option if needed

candidate_causes.cause: OCV/AOCV/POCV derating asymmetry at advanced nodes
candidate_causes.distinguishing_check: At ≤7nm, if hold violations appear only under POCV with statistical derating and not under flat OCV, variation modeling is the culprit. 28nm designs rarely see this severity. Check LVF-based derating.
candidate_causes.typical_fix: Tighten derate, add hold margin in CTS, use useful skew cautiously

candidate_causes.cause: Fast corner (FF/low-temperature) hold violation
candidate_causes.distinguishing_check: If hold violations appear only at FF corner (fast PVT), it is corner-specific. At 28nm, FF hold is usually easy; at ≤7nm with lower Vdd, FF hold can be the limiting corner.
candidate_causes.typical_fix: Add hold buffers targeting FF corner, ensure hold signoff includes worst-case fast corner

ordering_rationale: Cheapest-first: check path report to confirm fast-data vs skew (minutes), then check SDC for MC paths (minutes), then corner analysis (hours). Fix by data-path buffers which are cheap and localized; never fix hold by slowing the clock (destroys setup elsewhere).
classic_trap: Fixing hold by adjusting the clock period or by adding delay to the clock path. Clock-period changes break setup globally; clock-path delay hurts all paths reaching that flip-flop. Hold fix belongs on the DATA path only. Also, engineers often ignore hold until post-CTS, causing expensive ECO loops near tapeout.

symptoms: Static IR drop > 5% of Vdd (older nodes) or > 3% (≤7nm) in voltage map
Dynamic IR drop (transient droop) causing at-speed test failures, functional at lower frequency or higher Vdd
Hold violations cluster physically in regions coincident with IR-drop hotspots; setup violations may also appear if droop is severe

candidate_causes.cause: Weak power grid (strap width/pitch inadequate for current density)
candidate_causes.distinguishing_check: Static IR drop map shows broad, gradual voltage gradient peaking at farthest point from PG pad/ring. At ≤7nm, metal R is ~10x higher than 28nm, so this is the dominant cause. Strengthen grid and re-run static analysis; if drop reduces proportionally, confirmed.
candidate_causes.typical_fix: Widen power straps, reduce strap pitch, add upper-layer straps, stagger mesh

candidate_causes.cause: Insufficient decoupling capacitance near high-switching clusters
candidate_causes.distinguishing_check: Dynamic IR drop map shows sharp, localized transient droop correlated with high-toggle-rate regions (e.g., datapath during at-speed test). Static IR may look fine. Add decaps and re-run dynamic vector-based simulation; if droop peak reduces, confirmed.
candidate_causes.typical_fix: Insert decap cells near switching clusters, increase decap density, add on-chip decap library variants

candidate_causes.cause: Localized current hotspot (power density) due to high-activity logic placement
candidate_causes.distinguishing_check: Dynamic power analysis shows high current density in a region; correlate ATE fail logs with physical location — if failures are bursty and diffuse but cluster spatially, it is dynamic droop, not a logic defect. Activity-driven placement can mitigate.
candidate_causes.typical_fix: Activity-driven placement (move high-switching cells near PG trunks), clock gating, re-timing to spread switching

candidate_causes.cause: Package/board-level PDN weakness (bond wire/bump/PCB plane)
candidate_causes.distinguishing_check: On-die IR looks acceptable but system-level droop persists; Vdd rail monitoring on ATE shows droop correlated with package current. Bump-map or package model simulation reveals bottleneck. Requires package change.
candidate_causes.typical_fix: Add bumps, redesign package PDN, increase board-level decaps

candidate_causes.cause: Electromigration (EM) induced IR drop (long-term degradation)
candidate_causes.distinguishing_check: EM analysis shows current density violations on power rails; after burn-in, IR drop worsens. Distinguish from pure IR by EM signoff report. Fix requires wider metals/redundant vias.
candidate_causes.typical_fix: Widen power wires, add via arrays, use higher metal layers for power

ordering_rationale: First distinguish static vs dynamic using both analyses (hours each). Static grid weakness is cheapest to confirm and fix in floorplan; dynamic decap placement requires activity vectors and is more expensive. Package-level issues are checked last because they imply a respin.
classic_trap: Treating dynamic IR drop as a static-grid problem — engineer widens straps, spends days re-routing, but dynamic droop persists because the root cause is insufficient decoupling or switching-peak concentration. Another trap: at ≤7nm, assuming 28nm-style 5% IR budget is safe; advanced nodes require ≤3% budget due to lower Vdd and higher R.

symptoms: CTS does not converge: buffer count explodes, tool aborts or runs indefinitely
Post-CTS local skew exceeds target (e.g., >100ps in sky130, tighter at advanced nodes)
Massive hold violations appear immediately after CTS; clock insertion delay (latency) varies wildly across flops

candidate_causes.cause: Poor placement forcing long clock routes (dense regions, extreme distances)
candidate_causes.distinguishing_check: After CTS, examine clock tree DAG: if max insertion delay endpoint is physically far from clock source or in a congested region, placement is the root cause. CTS buffer depth is uneven. Rollback to placement and inspect.
candidate_causes.typical_fix: Improve placement (spread congested regions, bring flops closer to clock root), add placement guides

candidate_causes.cause: Skew group definition error (multi-domain/power-switch designs)
candidate_causes.distinguishing_check: If Reg2Reg and Reg2ICG violations concentrate on inter-domain paths, check that skew groups are correctly defined AND aligned with clock groups. Clock groups guide STA, skew groups guide CTS — mismatch is a subtle, common miss.
candidate_causes.typical_fix: Define proper skew groups, align with clock groups, add generated-clock constraints

candidate_causes.cause: ICG (integrated clock gating) cell placed far from its fanout cone
candidate_causes.distinguishing_check: Latency report shows max insertion delay path goes through an ICG located far from downstream flops. The ICG placement strategy is wrong. In the DAG, trace the path from clock root to ICG to sink.
candidate_causes.typical_fix: Place ICG near clock root or near its fanout centroid, add placement constraint on ICG

candidate_causes.cause: PVT corner mismatch: CTS targeted one corner, signoff at another
candidate_causes.distinguishing_check: If CTS was run at TT but worst violations appear at SS or FF, CTS optimized the wrong corner. Re-run CTS with worst-case extraction; at ≤7nm this is mandatory due to variation sensitivity.
candidate_causes.typical_fix: Run CTS with multi-corner optimization, use AOCV/POCV derating on clock tree cells

candidate_causes.cause: Useful skew overshoot: positive skew applied for setup has eaten hold margin
candidate_causes.distinguishing_check: If hold violations appear exactly on paths where useful skew was applied for setup, the skew budget is exhausted. Check skew group report for positive skew values; the sum of setup help equals hold cost.
candidate_causes.typical_fix: Rebalance: reduce positive skew, add data-path hold buffers, use useful skew only where setup truly needs it

candidate_causes.cause: Clock net shielding/NDR inconsistency leading to post-route skew degradation
candidate_causes.distinguishing_check: If skew is acceptable immediately post-CTS but degrades after detailed routing, clock nets were re-routed without NDR/shielding. Check clock net routing rules; compare pre-route and post-route skew.
candidate_causes.typical_fix: Apply NDR (double-width, double-spacing) and shielding on clock nets before routing, lock clock routes

ordering_rationale: CTS failure is primarily a placement-quality test — veterans rollback to placement FIRST (minutes to diagnose) before touching CTS knobs. Then check skew-group definition (minutes), then ICG placement (minutes), then corner alignment (hours). The ordering reflects that 80% of CTS failures are placement or constraint issues, not CTS engine issues.
classic_trap: Pushing CTS effort higher hoping the tool 'converges' when the underlying placement is broken — buffer count explodes, power skyrockets, and routing becomes impossible. The second trap: confusing clock groups (for STA) with skew groups (for CTS) in multi-domain designs, leading to inter-domain skew that no amount of buffering can fix.

symptoms: Spacing violations (most frequent): metal-to-metal distance < minimum rule
Minimum width violations: wires narrowed by router below minimum width rule
Via violations: missing/insufficient vias, single-via where array required
Short violations: overlapping routes, often from ECO patch routing or manual edits

candidate_causes.cause: Routing congestion causing spacing violations
candidate_causes.distinguishing_check: If DRC violations cluster exactly at congestion hotspots (overlay DRC markers on congestion map), it is congestion-induced. The router detoured into non-preferred tracks and violated spacing. Fixing DRC alone will not hold.
candidate_causes.typical_fix: Relieve congestion (see FAIL_CONGESTION), re-route with DRC-driven routing, enable spacing-driven detail route

candidate_causes.cause: Missing redundant vias (single via where DRC/minimum rules require array)
candidate_causes.distinguishing_check: DRC report shows 'via missing' or 'via enclosure' violations concentrated on power/clock nets. Automated routing used minimal vias. Via optimization was not enabled.
candidate_causes.typical_fix: Enable redundant-via insertion, use via arrays for power/clock, run via optimization post-route

candidate_causes.cause: ECO patch routing introducing shorts/overlaps
candidate_causes.distinguishing_check: If violations appear only in regions touched by recent ECO, and are 'short' or 'overlap' type, the ECO introduced geometry without re-legalization. Check ECO change list vs DRC location.
candidate_causes.typical_fix: Re-route ECO nets with legalization, avoid manual wire edits, run incremental DRC

candidate_causes.cause: Manual cell movement or manual wire editing bypassing router
candidate_causes.distinguishing_check: If violations are 'line-to-line' spacing at locations where cells/wires were manually moved, the router's legalization was bypassed. Cross-probe layout: manually edited regions show clean geometry but violate rules.
candidate_causes.typical_fix: Re-run legalization, revert manual edits, use router-controlled ECO

candidate_causes.cause: Rule deck / constraint mismatch (e.g., wrong metal layer rules applied)
candidate_causes.distinguishing_check: If violations are systematic across an entire layer or net type (e.g., all M3 wires), check that the routing rules match the foundry rule deck for that layer. 28nm vs ≤7nm have vastly different minimum rules; using wrong layer ruleset is common in hierarchical integration.
candidate_causes.typical_fix: Correct routing rule deck, re-run routing for affected layers/nets

candidate_causes.cause: Density violations (metal density below minimum) triggering fill requirement
candidate_causes.distinguishing_check: If violations are 'density' type in sparse regions, the design lacks dummy metal fill. Uneven distribution near macros or sparse routing areas.
candidate_causes.typical_fix: Insert dummy metal fill following foundry-recommended strategy, balance density across regions

ordering_rationale: Veterans classify DRC by type and location (minutes): overlay on congestion map to separate congestion-induced from local geometry errors. Congestion-induced requires floorplan/placement fix (expensive); local via/spacing errors can be auto-fixed quickly (minutes-hours). The ordering avoids blind 'fix-all-violations' loops that ignore root cause.
classic_trap: Running auto-DPR 'fix all DRC' which patches spacing violations by nudging wires, but the underlying congestion remains — new DRCs appear elsewhere, creating an infinite loop. The senior engineer first asks whether DRC violations are SYMPTOMS of congestion (fix floorplan) or local geometry errors (auto-fix is fine). At ≤7nm, ignoring DFM/DFY rules (CMP, litho hotspots) in DRC signoff leads to yield disasters even with 'clean' DRC.
